utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So, Madam Registrar, could you call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-05-88-T, the Prosecutor versus Vujadin Popovic et al.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, ma'am, and good afternoon to you. Is everyone here? Except Ms. Nikolic. Prosecution, Mr. Nicholls and Mr. McCloskey. No preliminaries, I take it. All right. Mr. Zivanovic, you had started your cross-examination yesterday. How long do you think -- how much time do you think you require?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I estimate until the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the rest? If you could give me a rough indication.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. President, Your Honours. A half hour for us approximately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Approximately 30 minutes, Mr. President. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Your Honours. We think it's going to be about 15 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] About 45 minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: Five minutes maximum, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: We will not ask anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can you repeat, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: We will not ask anything in cross.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And where is your colleague?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: I beg your pardon? I didn't hear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Where is Mr. Haynes?

utterances.speaker: MR. SARAPA
utterances.text: He's coming after the first break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Then we should be able to make it. We should be able to make it. Let's make an effort. If you try to cut down on yours, in particular, Mr. Popovic -- Mr. Zivanovic, we should be able to make it. Tomorrow we have the other witness coming back to finish his cross-examination. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The last question I put to you yesterday had to do with computers. You said you didn't know whether your computer was new or old. Could you please tell me whether it worked? Did it function properly, like the other equipment you used?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, quite normally. We didn't really have any problems. If there would be a problem, a solution would always be found to have another computer brought in.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, I did not quite understand yesterday your answer to the Prosecutor's question in relation to entering dates into the computer. Could you tell me whether that date was automatically typed into the computer or did it actually have to be typed out by the operator who was transcribing the text?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, in the morning, when a report would be made for the previous day, it would be sufficient if we would report to the command in the morning. That's when the date would be entered. And then perhaps a correction would be made, so the operator would do it and then just copy it for next -- every following file or report that was sent, perhaps. It wasn't automatically done.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So the computer did not automatically assign a date? Did the computer automatically assign numbers, though?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not that either. It was the operator who did that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we have a look at 1D82, please? This document is only in Serbian, a translation was asked for. It's relatively short, so I'd like to read it out. As you can see, this is SBKZ, 8th of July, 1995. It says: "During our last shift when we were taking over our duty on the 5th of July, 1995, around 1700 hours, the colleague in charge of working at the SBKZ conveyed to us that over the past few days, call-signs were being repeated. That could easily be proven because we have a paper with call-signs from the 3rd of June, 1995. We were wondering what this was about so we went further on. We returned the system date to the computer to the 9th of June, 1995, and carried out a normal procedure of forming signs for today through ABSIF.EXE and PRET.EXE and established that as for today, the 8th of July, 1995, it is the date of the 9th of June, 1995 that is being applied both in terms of" --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note that it was read out too fast. We have not finished the sight translation of the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you have in it in front of you, so you can -- Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't know yet again what the question will be but just to remind my friend some of these should perhaps not be broadcast publicly. It depends on where he's going, I suppose, but we just need to be careful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I mean, from my understanding, the practice dealing with these witnesses is that we don't broadcast but what I want to make sure, and I think I can make sure from the transcript, is that the location is not mentioned, and I don't think Mr. Zivanovic mentioned the location so we can safely go ahead. On the other hand, Mr. Zivanovic and everyone else for that matter, you don't need to read out the entire document. I mean, usually the witness is either already aware of it or he can have a look at it. It will be quicker. And then you can move to your question. So I suggest you move to your question straight away. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I read this out for the Trial Chamber because I only have the document in B/C/S so I thought that it was necessary to have the Prosecutor become aware of it as well as the Trial Chamber. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My question is as follows: Are you familiar with this document?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Most of the time the questions related to only part of the document so that's -- let's move. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you just tell me, please, whether you remember this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not remember this document, and I don't think that it's a document from my unit at all but, rather, the neighbouring signals unit that was at the facility. I'm unaware of it. This is the first time I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, VJ 5022/5, is that the symbol of your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I cannot confirm that for you because throughout all that time, I never looked at what the symbol or marking for my unit was.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Perhaps to jog your memory, could you have a look at the index that the Prosecutor showed you yesterday? That would be Prosecution Exhibit 13, 1357, for instance, or 1392, sorry, 1392, from the Prosecutor's list.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: I'm sorry, which one, 1392, A, B, C?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's from the 65 ter list, 1392; I think it's document E.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: There is no 1392 E.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] D.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, if I can help, I think the one -- my guess is the one that my friend wants is B, and I have a copy here or it can be brought up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, if that helps us speed up things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: We have it in Sanction.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No broadcast.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Microphone not activated]. The document can also be placed on the ELMO. You can take 1392 B.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Do you see the header, 5022/5, the same as that marking for your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, I see that, possibly. Well, I've read it again. This happened during a changeover between two shifts, when one squad was replacing the other. So this was a mistake, and obviously it was the preceding squad, the preceding shift, that had caused this mistake. The operators who were working on the computer, who knew about this much better than I did. I don't recall this document, but it is possible that the problem did crop up as described here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The document was signed by RPST. That is to say, the radio intercept station.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, it can be put that way.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Was this customary, to carry out such interventions on the computer, to return dates, say, a month or so?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that was the only time, because I certainly would have known had it ever happened again. I don't even remember this, so I cannot be more specific.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In the last part of this document, or not this document but the previous document, which I did not read out in order to save time, it says that the chief of security should be informed about this because it jeopardises the functioning of the unit. I assume that you bore that in mind when this was written, that you were made aware of this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that was a recommendation for the people down there, our leadership in the corps, to take some measures. What they did about this, I don't know. I really cannot remember that situation now after all that time.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Can you please look at 1D83 now. This is yet another report about the state of the technical equipment. As you can see again, it was sent by the radio intercept (redacted), this time on the 13th of July, 1995. In the first paragraph, it says that the computer disk is barely kept alive, and that yesterday, so that is to say on the 12th of July, you had to refresh it several times with some programmes. Then there is a description further on about the interference that is manifested and how it is manifested and towards the end of this paragraph it says that it would be far more convenient to do this -- or, rather, to resort to some system files if disk programme A would be functioning properly on the computer.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you aware of this report?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Specifically, this report, well, I can't remember it. I can't remember this one either. But from time to time, which is only natural, we had this kind of thing with computers, especially these older type computers, so it would happen that the disk would become oversaturated or whatever and the system had to be refreshed, renewed so that it would stay alive. But at any rate, this did not prevent us from working and from receiving our assignments normally, and, of course, certain shortcomings and problems would be redressed along the way. Sorry, let me just finish. It never says here that we could not go on working. It just says that our work was made more difficult, but it does not say anywhere that we could not work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: But it doesn't say how you worked, and that's what we are interested in, because we would like to come to a conclusion. That's why I'm putting these questions to you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, fine.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. So this deficiency was redressed. Could you please look at the second paragraph of this same report. In it, it says that one disk was damaged on one of the UHERs and therefore it could not be used at all, that you need regular supplies with reserve parts, spare parts, new tapes, there is no alcohol so you cannot clean the heads properly. And then the following sentence says: "That is certainly a reason why we have some recordings of conversations that can barely be understood or cannot be understood at all, while being listened to."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember problems of that kind coming up from time to time. However, it only worked to our detriment. If a conversation would not be understandable, then it could not be recorded or transcribed. That is to say, that we asked for this in order to work in the best possible way, to have the least number of problems possible, and you could see from our recordings that if we could not understand something, if something was unintelligible, we would state it, or that was unaudible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, we saw what was written down, we didn't manage to hear the tapes, but, all right, this is not the subject of our conversation. At any rate, you resolved the computer problem, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, of course we resolved it, and it's not just this one computer that was working at the facility. If there would be any major damage or breakdown, then a new computer would be brought in, if necessary, things like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you replace this computer?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably or a new disk was brought in or something else, but at any rate the problem was resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Could you please have a look at Defence Exhibit 1D86? That is a report from the 28th of July, 1995. It says it seems that what was expected to happen finally happened here with our disk at such and such a place. The computer cannot open from the disk itself but only from system diskettes. The only message we get is no room for system on destination disk and so on. Do you remember whether that happened with the new computer that you got or the repaired one?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, probably the same one but I cannot say for sure either way. I mean, now I cannot even say how many times the computer was replaced. It's been a long time. So I cannot say whether it is that computer or some other computer, but I assume that it's the same one with which we had problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: At any rate, you did have a problem on that day, as we see?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes. Of course. It is normal to have problems in one's work and to resolve them and to go on. Could we please just have a look to this to the very end so maybe we'll find things clearer that way? Yes, you see in continuation the text says that it was possible to work but with great difficulty, which means that there was no interruption in the work, and then there are further instructions as to how the problem should be resolved.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: To be more precise, the sentence is as follows: If this is done properly, then for a certain period of time, we will have a faulty but a provisional solution, but I fear that something worse could happen.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but nothing specific is stated to the effect that it was not possible to work.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I have noticed that this report could not be sent that same day so that it was repeated on the 29th of July. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: After so much time, no, but we see who signed this report. This is a person who was in charge of the correspondence. I didn't interfere with his work. He knew what he had to do and how he should act, and he was far more expert than me in the area so that I never interfered with his work, and I knew that he would always do what was best.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I just ask, because I can't read the document, is that -- is there a separate document which shows that or is it contained somewhere in here? This is a disadvantage I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think you can glean it from this document that we have on the screen now because obviously Mr. Zivanovic is referring to the day after, which is the 29th of July, so he must be referring to another separate different document.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Could I just have some reference for that document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly, by all means. I was going to ask that myself. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I do have it printed out here. Thinking that it was one and the same document, I made an error and didn't propose it for Sanction, but it can be put on the ELMO and then we can compare this document with the one on the monitor because we'll see that the only difference is the header, the registration number, and the date. I can of course offer this to be placed under the ELMO and then the witness will see that the text is absolutely identical.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: My friend doesn't necessarily need to do that. I would just like to see it. I want to get a copy of it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or he can give us the ERN number and that should be enough. If you give us the ERN number, I think that should be enough, Mr. Zivanovic. Although today I'm beginning to doubt about the relevance of this set of questions because they relate to the 28th and the 29th, in relation to a particular machine, when we may be talking or should be concentrating on other days and other material maybe. But it's up to you, I'm not stopping you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. Let me give you the number: 0320-4900. That is the ERN number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us please have a look at the Defence Exhibit 1D93. This is a complaint from which it follows that three files sent on the previous day, that the first of that -- those files didn't reach its destination. Is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me just read it, please. That is what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As it is just a single sentence, allow me to read it. The document is dated the 3rd of August, 1995, and it says: "By comparing the OX files (protocol) I have established that you have not received our first report file of yesterday," and we have the figures in brackets, "according to the protocol, and which according to my records was sent in our first contact at 1133, when my two other files were sent and the codes are given. That is why I am sending you in attachment the same file that was missing." Do you remember this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not check the work of this operator. This is what he stated, and I believe him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please see that this file is strictly confidential 02028, dated the 2nd of August, 1995? That that is the file, this one that we see below and that file contains a certain report; is that right? You can look further down and you will see that -- what this file contained. Then it is a report dated the 2nd of August; several reports, actually. I think there are three of them.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. More or less, that is what it appears to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You can look at the next page too.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Well, I can see these two now. It's okay. Let me turn back now to the previous page, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we please turn back the monitor to the previous page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: A little lower down, further down. No. I want to see the header, please. It's okay now. As I can see things, I don't think that's quite right. It says here that I have established that you have not received our first report, and this is report number 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: It says here by comparing things I see that you have not received that -- that the addressee, and now you're sending the same report again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but our first report from yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Oh, I see, the 2nd of August.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Just a moment, please. This is not the first. This is the second. I don't know what the first file contained. This is the second file. Strictly confidential number 02. It is number 2, not number 1. It's not the first file. And then comes the third and the fourth. So what is missing is the first file, and it says here the first file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: My understanding is that this was your first file?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, but this is not the first file. It is the second one you're showing me. I'd like you to show me the first one so we can compare things, so we can see what the first file contained, because we have here the second, third and fourth file.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You see these files are coded, so I don't have the coded files, nor do I have the codes of those files. All I see is that you wrote that your first reporting file for that day did not reach the addressee.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. There are -- there is a doubt. It doesn't say that it wasn't received. There is a doubt as to whether it was received. So I don't know whether it is being repeated. I can't conclude from this that it is the first file because the first is missing here. We have the second, third and fourth file. I think we need to ask the operator about this because I can't be absolutely certain about these things.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to switch on to something else. Mr. Nicholls, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry, two points. One, my friend said "you wrote." I want to be clear that's nowhere in the record this was written by the witness, he talked about operator, the operator sending this. And second, I don't know if we can be told when we might get translations of these because it's very difficult. We are in a bad position trying to follow this in B/C/S. I appreciate it's not always easy to put together your list in advance, but especially with this witness, there were weeks and weeks of notice. The Paket was delivered sometime ago of the relevant intercepts and I don't think there were any surprises whatsoever in my testimony, so if these could come sooner it would be helpful.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm sure Mr. Zivanovic is working on that. Yes, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. Let me tell you, we did indeed receive a certain number of documents, but the documents that I'm asking questions about now, referring to the period we are interested in, July and August 1995, and the period covered by the indictment against my client, we have managed to find some but we haven't received them from the Prosecution. According to our understanding, these should be documents under Rule 68. Regarding the functioning of the equipment for that particular period, we feel it's rather important for properly judging the relevance and authenticity of all this. I was unable to provide the translations of these documents because they are outside the Srebrenica collection, they are not part of the Srebrenica collection, and that is the reason why we are unable to hand it in for translation earlier. It is now in the process of being translated. And we are in the hands of the translation service now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Does that satisfy you, Mr. Nicholls? Forget about the Rule 68 applicability or otherwise, I do not want anyone to get engaged in that discussion at this moment. I suggest we have heard enough on this, Mr. Zivanovic, and you can move to your next question, or next topic you would like to put to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like, Your Honour, to ask the witness to explain to us the meaning of these incomprehensible words which are the same as the code of the file which could not be provided. I'm --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If he knows, you can ask him yourself.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If he knows, if he knows.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You can ask the question. Why should we ask the question? You ask him the question directly. Please refer him to the particular parts from the text, the --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you please see that under the dotted line, there are the letters TBTD 28 NB and this is identical with the letters for the file which, according to this report, did not reach the unit it was addressed to.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As far as the symbols are concerned, I never knew what symbols the operator used. You should really ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I didn't ask you about the symbol itself. I'm just asking whether it is identical to the one in the text.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. So it could be that, but I didn't do it so I can't claim anything with certainty.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, what is the significance of the text below? Is it the content of what has been packed into this coded message?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: From all of this, it could be that but I can't say that that is what it actually is. It could be the complete report.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: These reports were sent in a certain sequence. You send those reports daily, if I understood you correctly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, naturally. Sometimes a day would go by when, except for the regular report, there were no other reports because there were no appropriate informations. It doesn't mean to say that we sent reports every single day.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So tell me, after this OT should be followed by 03, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, there has to be a proper order, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me, if that's the way it is, how was that report sent at 1133?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that means that by 1133 there was nothing to be sent, and it's only natural that it was sent when information was collected and processed and then it was sent on. We didn't have a particular time when we were supposed to send certain reports. This one was sent at 1133.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Which one, 03?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, there are different reports that were sent, 02, 03. 04 was probably the next one; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This was the first contact. Yes. Sent yesterday at 1133, according to the records established by the operator.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So three files were sent?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, when my -- well, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, if the first file was 02, the next one was 03, and then the one after that 04, right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that would only be natural, I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now, tell me, file 03, is a report about a recorded conversation carried out at 1240 and at 1300 hours. How come it was sent at 1133? Explain that to me.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, would you really have to ask the operator. I didn't send that. I mean, as for these finer points, I really don't know. I cannot understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: In other words, it is possible to send a conversation before it had been recorded?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know about that but, I mean, as for clarifying this matter, it can only be done by the operator. I mean, now I cannot really go into this, well, perhaps if I had a bit more time, if I'd have a better look and if I gave it some thought, then I could draw a conclusion perhaps, but it's not for me to -- well, it's not my job.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: All right. Let's not deal with that now then.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I was not doing that, so I cannot say.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, we saw several notebooks here and we saw the notebooks kept by your platoon. We can now have a look at 2316, for instance. So that I don't describe it for you, it's a Prosecution Exhibit, P2316. Could we just have a look at the next page, please? Another one, another one, please. Could you just get it right? No, not that one, no. Could you please get the first page back, or, rather, the third one? Page 3. Yes, yes, that's it. Before we received an explanation that usually every notebook or, rather, practically all notebooks were marked strictly confidential. Do you recall that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, my officers down there at the corps command put the numbers there, wrote this. We didn't. We just get a notebook with that written in, the number and --

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you. This shows that this is an official notebook.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's the way it should be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: As for this date, the 14th of June, that was the date when it was registered in the command; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps write this date, the 14th of June?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. That was written down at the command. They put the number too. We just get the notebooks this way, verified this way, numbered this way. We didn't do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Further on, we were informed that the notebook would be filled out on that day or, say, not exactly from that day when it was registered in the command but some date after that when they would bring it to your platoon; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's only logical that it couldn't be done before.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Tell me, please, were tapes marked the same way?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think so. I don't think the tapes were marked at all, but I cannot say anything for sure.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I'll try to jog your memory. Could the witness please be shown 2315? Prosecution Exhibit 2315. The page is 7967. That's the ERN number. 7915. And what we have on the screen is 16. 7967.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Nothing, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you see the number that's up here after the frequency, 791, and then three zeros? Is that the number of the tape?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that it's more probable that it can be the number of some notebook, but I cannot say that either one is absolutely correct.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we have a look at page 70, please? 7970, that is. What does it say here? Is that the number of the tape, tape 08/2-01-140?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what's written here, tape, yes, well, possibly. I mean, a few moments ago I didn't say that it was or that it wasn't, but now we see it's the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Please have a look at the next page. I'm sorry, it seems that it's not that one. Could you just lower it a bit? The next page, please? Here, 72, I'm sorry, does it say tape 08/2 again?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That's what it says, tape 08/2.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Now I can show you five other pages where it invariably says that it's such and such a tape with that number, but if you don't --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not necessary.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I don't really want to waste time. I did not notice that the tapes were marked, as far as the intercepts were concerned, of conversations between General Krstic and Popovic.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please put that question again?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I was saying that I did not notice that in that conversation that you transcribed, that you marked the tape number concerning the conversation between Krstic and Popovic. If you need to have a look at it again, that's no problem.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It's not necessary. As far as I managed to see, right now, in a hurry, I know that usually we didn't write down the tape numbers. And as far as I could see, in this hurry, I think it's the same operator, it looks like the same handwriting, who, for reasons unknown to me, wrote the tape number too. But if you look at a series of other transcripts, you will not find the tape number anywhere. It is possible that this one particular operator -- well, I'm doing all of this in a hurry. As far as I managed to notice, it was this one particular operator who did that, but on many others you're not going to find the tape number.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You're right on that. I just have a different question, though. You say that the tapes were not marked. However, this shows that the tapes did have numbers. I assume that the operator did not just invent a number on his own.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't think so either, but tapes were tapes for me, and I really never looked at them very carefully to see whether they had numbers or not, because we brought many tapes from different companies and now whether they had all been numbered, well, probably so. That seems to be the case. But I simply cannot remember.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: By the way, I asked you about these notebooks and I asked you about that first date in them but I forgot to ask you about many of these notebooks. We saw at the end a particular date and that would usually be the date when that notebook would be finished. It was not in all notebooks to be quite fair, but in many notebooks, at the end, there is a date when it was finished. Usually the one-but-last page. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never did that, but it's possible that operators did that on their own. They did not receive such orders from me, that they would state when a particular notebook would be finished or completed. Had we known that all of this would happen, we really would have done all of these things but we had no idea. We used the notebooks only in order to help us. Later on we typed this out into the computer and send it on to whoever we were supposed to send this on. We did not really pay any attention to these notebooks in terms of protocol, numbering, signatures and so on. Had we known about that, then certainly after everyone of these transcripts we would have stated the name and surname of everyone who did that and perhaps we would give some other details too. I mean, this is something that was just there to assist us.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Witness, you need to answer in a more brief and concise manner because otherwise we are not going to finish with you in time. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just want to correct the record, Your Honour, and ask counsel to be a little bit careful when he's saying what the witness stated. He misstated what the witness's first answer was to the question of whether tapes were marked. The witness said exactly what he said later, that he wasn't sure, not that they weren't. He's tried to change this into some kind of direct flat out no on his part which is just sort of -- that he be careful. And I think the witness is trying to explain his answers. This is taking a long time, but I think it's partly the nature of the questions that he feels he needs to explain.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, but anyway, he has already, as regards your first remark, I think he has reiterated his position. The rest I'm asking the witness to be brief, as brief as possible, in his answers because otherwise -- I mean, try not to give more details than you are actually being asked to give because that would keep you here longer than we would like to see you here. So let's go ahead, Mr. Zivanovic, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I think that you actually did not understand what it was that I said. I did not mention that on the last pages that the operators wrote dates. As far as we understood things, at least on the basis of statements made by some of your other colleagues, these dates were entered in the unit command when the notebooks were returned. You probably never saw these notebooks once they were returned.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Well, that's an explanation then. Could you please have a look at the first page now, precisely of this notebook that we are dealing with now, or rather, the second page. So that would be -- yes, there is it. So on page 1, the date is the 14th of April, 1995. Could we now look at the one-but-last page? Thank you. Do you see that the date indicated is the 17th of June, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Can you explain how is it that we see such dates in this notebook, dates following the 17th of June, 1996?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Yesterday the Prosecutor read out to you a summary of what you had discussed with him. Among other things, it is stated there that you had heard the audiotapes. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. A tape recorder was brought in and I listened to the tape.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You did this in the Prosecutor's office prior to your testimony?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, 10 days before, then yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And you heard the identical sounds that we heard in the courtroom here yesterday?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I heard the conversation that I heard on a certain date in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You said, among other things, that this conversation left a very strong impression on you so that you will remember it to the end of your days; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you tell me what it is that left such an impression on you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In those days, when that conversation was recorded, it was already known what was happening in and around Srebrenica, and we were all quite shocked by this. And when I heard this conversation, I realised that there was a hunt continuing, a hunt for men, and this demand for those men to be brought back, it was known what would happen to those men if they were returned, and that is why I will always remember it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: When you say that it was known what would happen to them if they were returned, can you be more specific?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I'll tell you: That they would be killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Tell me, please, in those days, do you remember, you certainly remember, that quite a large group, in fact all the population from Zepa, had been evacuated to free Muslim territory without any loss of human life; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Tell me what period you're referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: The period when you heard this conversation.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Why then were you afraid that these people would be treated in a different way from the people of Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know who is asking such questions. We know who crossed into free territory and we also know how many people never reached free territory, nor will they. And the whole world knows this, not just me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: So nevertheless your conclusion was that these men would be executed if they were returned to Republika Srpska?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely so. Otherwise, why did the general ask for them to be returned? Because he loved them?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Perhaps he wanted to exchange them with someone.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You made a statement on the 17th and 18th of November, 1999, to the investigators of The Hague Tribunal. Remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume your memory was better then than it is today.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Do I need to comment? I don't know. We'll see. I don't know what you're going to ask me.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: You said then that you remember a few conversations and, if necessary, I can let you read this out. But in brief, this is what you said: "Krstic and Popovic talked about cleansing. I think it was about 9.00. And the conversation was about two days after the fall of the enclave. Krstic said something to the effect that they shouldn't leave anyone alive and Popovic answered something to the effect, Don't worry, boss, that's what we are doing." Do you remember those words that you said?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Did you take -- note down that conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. But at the time the conversation was going on, I was sitting next to a colleague, and I heard the conversation, and that colleague was noting it down.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: This was in 1998, is that right, or 1999?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1999. At the time I had already forgotten some things, and I think that this conversation was not with Mr. Popovic but with Mr. Obrenovic. It was Obrenovic and Krstic. And I think it is true. But that is how I recalled it at the time and that is why I gave that statement to the investigator lady who was there at the time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is a difference between -- it's important to know whether it was -- he mentioned Popovic, as you suggested to him, or he mentioned Obrenovic, as he is suggesting now. If you can refer us precisely to the part from his testimony in Krstic. You first suggested to him that it was -- that he had mentioned -- referred to a conversation between Krstic and Popovic. And now -- initially he sort of agreed with you, or at least he remembered the occasion, and he even gave details. But he is correcting one very important aspect of it and that is that it wasn't Popovic but it was Obrenovic. So I think you need to refer him to the specific part of his testimony. We see it as well. And everyone else. And then if it's the case of proceeding with further questions, of course, please go ahead. If not, we switch on to the next question. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think he's referring to the witness statement, not the testimony.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It is a statement, yeah, all right. So can we show him the statement, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes. It is 5D156. Page 4. 5D156.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: We don't have anything as 5D156.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have the hard copy, Mr. Zivanovic?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, it's 5D146.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I said 5D.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 146 and not 156. Which page in the B/C/S language, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation].

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Page 4, in both the English and B/C/S versions. Towards the bottom of the page. Yes, we can see it, at the very bottom. "I also remember a couple of other conversations from approximately the same period."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I can give you an answer without looking. I know that that is what I said, what I told the Court's investigator, because this wasn't a conversation that I recorded but I heard it before the operator started taking it down in the notebook. He let me and our other colleagues hear it once again and when I made this statement, recalling that conversation, I attributed it to Mr. Popovic. However, later, I realised, when I was looking through the materials I had recorded, I know with certainty now that it wasn't General Krstic and Mr. Popovic, but General Krstic with Mr. Obrenovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: I assume you've seen that it is the paragraph marked with 1, towards the bottom of the page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. No. I don't want to interfere. It's okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Let us also examine something else that you mentioned. You mention here the conversation that was discussed yesterday, and I see that at the time you knew that this was happening after the fall of Zepa, as is stated here in paragraph 2, same page, same document, under point 2, and it begins with the words "after the fall of Zepa."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: And then you explain that these were people who had fled to Bajina Basta and so on. So at the time you knew that Zepa had fallen and that you were referring to people from Zepa?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. When Zepa fell, everything else around it had to fall before that, because Srebrenica was the last to fall. It was logical that Zepa should fall before that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Are you certain of that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I wouldn't like to claim anything. It's just my logical thinking.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Thank you, thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: When what fell I don't think is -- I simply didn't follow those things.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Zivanovic. Who is going next? Mr. Ostojic, who is appearing for Colonel Beara will be cross-examining you next.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, good afternoon. I'm going to ask you a series of questions.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: First I would like to -- you mentioned in your direct evidence today that, or yesterday, I should say, on page 12, lines 11 -- 17 through 20, that you were certified and you were certified in the B category as an amateur ham operator; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had C, B and A.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The highest classification for a ham operator is the A category; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is there a distinction between a B classification and an A classification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Is it significant or can you share with us what that distinction or difference is, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, perhaps it will take a bit of time if I explain all this, but there is a difference in the level of knowledge about electronics, radio devices, and also the speed of receiving and transmitting Morse code. There is a difference.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think the difference is not only in the level of knowledge, the experience, training and the expertise that one would attain in order to get that A category certification; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Unless you had a certain level of professionalism, you wouldn't get this class A classification. I never gave it to anyone, so I can't really say anything more.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, sir. Now in your statement that you gave to the OTP on November 17th and 18th, 1999, you listed some people in your squad, and I would like to ask you with respect to each of these individuals to the best of your recollection, which ones, if any, had maintained any level of certification as an amateur radio ham operator. But before we do that, I think we should go into private session so that you could list off their names.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So if we may go into private session, Your Honour, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's do that, yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, can you describe for us the procedures or standards governing intercept operators while trying to identify speakers on purported intercept conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The identity of a speaker was primarily established through his introducing himself in the first place. But if they didn't introduce themselves and both I and the operators were certain that this was a particular person, then it would be noted that the conversation was between such and such; or if we knew about one participant we would give his name and the other one would be given a number or a letter; and if both were unknown, then numbers would be attributed to them, 1, 2, or 3, if there were several collocutors, or maybe letters.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So am I fair to summarise the only way you as an intercept operator were able to identify the speaker was one of two ways: One, if the speaker introduced himself; or (b), during the conversation if the speaker or one of the persons speaking identified the person to whom he was speaking. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Precisely so. And also, on the basis of their voices. We sometimes knew by the voice who it belonged to. Sometimes not, but in many cases we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And I think yesterday you mentioned something to that effect. I think you used the term voice modulation on page 35; I believe it's lines 10 through 20. Do you know, sir, what voice modulation is?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In radio ham traffic, we used this term "modulation," implying the colour of the voice, the level of voice. When we say that it is over-modulated, it means that the voice sounds as if it's coming through a whistle. Or if it's low modulation, it doesn't carry very well. So the modulation describes the condition of the voice. That is our jargon. In our terminology, that is the term we used. We would say the modulation of your voice is such and such. If it's not good, then we indicate that something should be done about it, because poor modulation can be caused by poor devices and a poor microphone.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: All right. Well, sir, are you familiar with what the characteristics or the criteria that is utilised by forensic linguistics or phonetics experts in determining voice recognition or voice identification?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was never involved in those areas except for the past few years. When working as a radio ham operator, I use a computer which uses a programme to record, and then we can follow the voice frequency. But I'm no expert in the area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I was just going to point out that that's exactly what the witness said on his direct, that he said he wasn't an expert, so it's not really fair to ask him --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but he also explained. I mean, I couldn't let you speak because he had already started answering the question when you stood up. But at the same time, at least he's given us some fresh information, that this is an area which he has improved upon now, an area of knowledge. It seems that in the last few years he's gained more information than he had before. But certainly he didn't have this information or knowledge before, or expertise.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If I may proceed, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct in understanding from the Krstic testimony that's been introduced into evidence that you were never given an order or directive to identify speakers during your work as an intercept operator in July and August of 1995; is that correct? Oh, I'm sorry, page 8820. Of the Krstic testimony, sorry.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember that anyone gave an order to us to do that. But judging by the sound of the voice, having heard Krstic, for instance, dozens of times, we all knew when he started speaking that it was him. There was no need to have any proof of that, just as I can recognise my friends when they call me up.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand, but I just want to confine what your duties and obligations were in July and August of 1995. Sir, am I correct that you were never instructed by your commanders or any superior to actually record or to identify the speakers in a purported intercept conversation?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'd ask him to break that up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One he has already asked. But -- and more or less we've had the answer. So perhaps he can ask the second part of the question, because we've heard enough on the first one.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, is it true that the reason you weren't in fact given an order or a directive to identify speakers on these purported intercept conversations was because someone else in a different unit would digest that information and they would analyse that information to determine several things or different things, such as the value of that information, the reliability of that information, and whether or not that information is actually accurate. Correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I don't think he can be asked to say why he was not given an order and then speculate on this other long line of the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, you need to rephrase your question and ask him whether he is aware of another unit which did precisely what you think they were doing.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you aware of another unit who was actually digesting the contents of these purported intercept conversations that you were working on in July of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would put it as follows: No, not another unit. There were a certain number of people in my unit who worked and who were attached to the corps command, and I was convinced that they did that but I didn't have insight into what they were doing. So that is as much as I can say. I do know that there were personnel who did this because there would be no reason for us to send tapes away from our facility and all the notebooks from the facility somewhere. We could have just thrown them away or burned them or something.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues]... before the break, if I may ask you this. Sir, were you ever given or did you maintain, I should say, a list during July and August of 1995 of code-names of various relay stations or names of VRS officers while you were conducting these intercepts operational duties?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. We never received that. We just recorded the conversations and forwarded them. The command may have done something to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just one last question before the break. I think it should be about time for the break. One last question, sir: Did you -- were you ever given or any members of your unit down in the southern area where you were, were you ever give a dossier or any information regarding the background or any specific information regarding any VRS officers that you were purportedly intercepting conversations from?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: It might be convenient now, Your Honour, if you don't mind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So we need to have a 30-minute break because we redacted a part in the course of this first session, so it's quarter past 4.00 that we will reconvene. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, thank you, sir. Just to proceed, we were discussing briefly the testimony that you gave in the Krstic case, specifically page 8820, where you stated that there were no orders or directives to identify the speakers. Now, also with respect to that you were asked by the Judge in that case, sir, same page for my learned friends, line 17 through 21, whether sometimes you compared intercepts, and your answer, sir, was: "Well, no, I don't remember comparing them because, quite simply, the message was recorded and then it was transcribed into the notebook from the tape, from the notebook into the computer, and it was dispatched to the headquarters and command, or whenever we sent it on, and we did not go back to those conversations again." My question to you, sir, in connection with that answer that you gave, if you could help clarify it, am I correct that the intercept operators never verified or double-checked the information that was being sent to the higher command to determine whether or not the information that was being given was correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We did not check anything. Once we'd send our information on, that would have been a done thing for us, as far as that information was concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I saw you unsure on your feet, whether you wanted to object or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No, again, Your Honour, I was going to object to the phrasing of the question based on the transcript in Krstic because the question in Krstic was only about comparing intercepts, but I chose to let it just flow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Yes, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, in your statement, again November 17th and 18th of, 1999, you discussed that you did not have notebooks and I think you said 1993 until late 1994 and that you kept the information that you would -- or the conversation that is you would intercept on pieces of paper and then you would throw those papers away, correct, or they would be burned, I think you said. Right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And in late 1994 you began receiving notebooks and you were told to actually save them; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so that I can understand the specific procedure, is it correct, sir, that before transcribing the purported conversations into these notebooks the operators would take notes on various pieces of paper in order to remember the details of those conversations; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: In principle, yes. Well, you mentioned here these notes on pieces of paper, but usually we'd have these papers with things typed out on them, like workers councils' meetings and so on, but then you could write on the other side. So what you said, various pieces of paper, notes, well, it's not right. Well, you know, we didn't really just use little pieces of paper. It wasn't that we weren't working seriously.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Forgive me if you got that impression. I wasn't suggesting that you weren't working seriously or that you had small pieces of paper. Taking that aside, whether the paper was large or small, am I correct that your process was to jot down notes of the conversation on this -- these pieces of paper, large or small, and from those notes you would then transcribe them into this book that we have seen the originals of here, and then from that book they would be actually typed out in this computer that we talked about, and then it would be sent to the command. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no. You are now comparing these little pieces of paper or, rather, pages from the notebook. When we had these sheets of paper, there weren't any notebooks. Let's get that clear. As for the audio recordings from the tapes, we listened to them and then wrote things down on those sheets and then copied that into the notebooks. And then from there, we would copy them on to the computer. These pieces of paper were used as an auxiliary tool, just like the notebooks, because ultimately we were supposed to type this out on the computer and send it further on to the command.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And am I correct, then, in understanding that these pieces of paper that were used as auxiliary tools they have been subsequently destroyed; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Until the notebooks appeared, they were destroyed. They were burned as a rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, let me ask you if I could explain this to me, sir: You mentioned that when you listened to audio taped conversations, and if you were uncertain or unclear of what was said, that several intercept operators would gather together to determine what was actually said in the conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, was there a standard or a guideline in order to inform the command to whom you were sending these conversations, to advise them that it was a difficult conversation, that many people listened to it, that we had to listen to it several times? Were you instructed to keep those types of notes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Nothing was instructed. We simply stated things in notebooks. You can see that. If we did not hear something, we did not hear it. If it was unintelligible, we would say that it's unintelligible. We didn't do anything else apart from that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: The question is, sir, and from looking at these notebooks do you indicate in any of those notebooks which conversations were difficult to understand at the first hearing, the second, or fifth hearing? Do you give any indication whatsoever whether the conversation was difficult to intercept and understand or easy to intercept and understand?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that that was never recorded. It would be highlighted in the text itself. If you could not hear a word, then in place of that word you'd say, "inaudible," "unintelligible" or something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, if we can turn to a quick subject, the nicknames that you heard various people use in the intercepted conversation. Do you know if different men had the same nickname from time to time back in July and August of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't think I know that. Well, many people did not have nicknames and then many people did have nicknames, and that's the way they would address each other and then we would use the same term, the same term that we would hear.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: This in the one intercept, sir, that we discussed I think yesterday with my learned friend in your direct examination, or examination-in-chief, you mentioned the nickname Zoki, and I think you added that the name actually meant Zoran because it was a nickname of someone. But that nickname can mean several other things. People with different names other than Zoran could be named Zoki or called Zoki; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. But as for this conversation that we discussed yesterday, you hear it very nicely, the other collocutor says find Zoki, by Zoki, so he addressed him personally. If that was a code-name, then I was wrong.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you for that. Let me -- if we can turn to P023814 [sic], which I think is 65 ter number 1138A. And maybe the original book would also be helpful, if we could place that on the ELMO as well for the witness, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that's possible, Madam Registrar, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you. It was Prosecutor's -- I'll repeat the number, P02314, and specifically within that it's 65 ter number 1138A, as in apple. Do you have that book?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I believe 2314 was the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I may have reversed those numbers and didn't change that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You had corrected that too.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, I didn't note that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2314 is the pseudonym sheet.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then it's reversed. It should be 2313, Your Honour, I apologise. I didn't note that in --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2313 is the transcript.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: You're maybe looking for 2315.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2313 is the transcript of the testimony, 2314 is the pseudonym sheet. What 2315 is I have to check and then I can tell you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Then it's my fault, Your Honour, because I'm using an old version of the OTP's sheet.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: 2315 is handwritten intercept notebook, number 231.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the one you wanted?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Yes. And the ERN number, which we looked at yesterday, showing 01077918, which is the 13th of July, 1995, that the witness discussed yesterday. And if we could have the original placed on the ELMO as well, it would help. Perfect.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, the Honourable Judge Kwon asked you yesterday about this date on the second page following the intercept that you were led into evidence by the Prosecutor, and on the bottom of that 14.07.95; do you see that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: If we look at the original, sir, am I correct in noting that that's in the same pencil or ink pen that the entire intercept was recorded; correct? And I invite to you look at the original.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, I see it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So it's rather reasonable that in fact it was your writing, 1407, at the conclusion of this intercept; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Possibly. But, well, it's not 100 per cent sure that I write my 4s this way but, well, it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, what I'm interested in also in addition to that is that the next entry is what date, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 16th of July, 1995.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you tell us, sir, why the 15th of July, 1995, is not recorded anywhere in this book?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, after the question was put yesterday, I mean with regard to this same case, I gave this a bit of thought, and it is obvious that, well, since there were at least two notebooks for the intercepts, it's evident, it's a fact, that as for this notebook, on the 14th and 15th not a single conversation was recorded. Probably there was very little traffic. You'd either have to look for the other notebook and to look up information from the 14th and 15th in this other notebook and see-- well, we were not duty-bound to use both notebooks so that the dates would coincide. We didn't really think about that at the time, but it is certain that you will find information from the 14th and 15th in the other notebook. It is not to say that there was no information, well, that possibly there was no information but sometimes for a few days there would simply be no information. There would be some information that was unimportant, that was of a private nature and so on.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I understand. And sir, let me just understand the process a little better. When you had these receivers and mixers and the Kenwood TS-450, did you have one notebook assigned to a specific receiver, or did the operator, can he go from receiver to receiver to jot down information that he was intercepting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it's evident from the notebooks themselves. One conversation after the other as they were recorded and obviously it's not from the same device. Well, we didn't have any need to -- well, quite simply, the operator would use the notebook that was there at hand, that was closer to him. Perhaps the other one was being used for having something typed out. It wasn't that there was just one notebook for one device. On that day we would use, say, two notebooks until we filled them out. It didn't matter in what order information was coming in.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Then explain, if you can, the front of the book, what's the references that you make to like the RRU-800 or the type of receiver that the information was taken from for that specific book. If you don't mind turning to the front cover of the original that's before you and explain that to me, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, as for this notebook that I have here now, I don't know if that's the one you're talking about, the number is 3, that's what it says here. That's probably its number. RRU-800, 20 -- the 6th of June, 1995. The 11th of August, 1995. That's what it says here.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: So can we agree that that information that's on the front of the book is attributed to a specific receiver or specific mixer upon which you were obtaining these intercepted conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that this was the date when this notebook was inaugurated because you can see it on the first page, and then I didn't check but the other date is probably the one when it was concluded. It's not the number of devices or equipment or whatever.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Just so the record is clear, when you say "first page," you're saying the inside, not the front cover of the book, but on the inside first page of the book; correct? Or second page, or whatever it is. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, the first date is the 20th of June, 1995, as it says here on page 5.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Sir, I want to talk a little bit about in the few minutes that I have about receiving intercepts in their proper context. Now, you weren't an analyst; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Now, in the Krstic trial, when you testified, and because it's in evidence I want to ask you a question, on page 8807, line 24, you were in that case, sir, asked to review, I think, three intercepts, two of which you discussed with us today, and then another intercept at 10.00 between Krstic and a guy, a person called Mandzuka. Do you remember that at all?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, in that, on page 8807, line 24, although you tell us in that testimony that that wasn't your handwriting, in order to keep the conversations in proper context when you talk about Krstic and others at 12.00 or 12.45 which follow that conversation, isn't it true that in that conversation, when it was read by the Prosecutor in that case, that evidence clearly showed that Krstic is telling Mandzuka to register the Muslims over there so they can be used for "exchange"? Do you remember that, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember the content of the conversation now, but I remember the name of Mandzuka being mentioned and I remember reading that, but now we would have to read it again. I would have to read it. I told you -- or, rather, I said then that I was not the one who intercepted that conversation and I'm not the one who recorded it in the notebook. It was done by another operator. I do not recall the content.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And we, just for the sake of clarity in the record, on page 8807, sir, page 5, the Prosecutor Mr. McCloskey after giving leave of court by

utterances.speaker: JUDGE RODRIGUES CONTINUES AND STATES
utterances.text: "All right. The first conversation at 10.00 a.m. is between Mandzuka and General Krstic, 862 A."
