Then he proceeds to quote the conversation, and he -- I can quote it all but I'm specifically interested in the quote at 23 and -- line 23 and 24 where he says, under quote, K, presumably for Krstic, as follows: "Register all RS/Republika Srpska/Muslims over there so we can use them for exchange. How many more are down there?" There is more there obviously, Your Honour, but in the interests of time I want to focus on that. That's the testimony that was read to you by the Prosecutor in Krstic. Given that, sir, having that testimony, and understanding that conversations should be kept in their proper context, the next two conversations in Krstic you talk about the intercepted version of your conversation between Krstic and Mr. Popovic, and you state that you thought it meant something else other than exchange. Am I correct, sir, that in fact if you read the intercepts in their proper context and do not take them piecemeal out of order or out of context, you would be in a better position to make a reasonable determination of what those conversations mean. Correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the order of all events, I think that hardly anyone would be naive enough to believe the sincerity of General Krstic when he said that. I didn't believe it myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. Let me ask you this, sir, about changing letters, and I think yesterday on page 39, line 1 through 5, you stated: "There may have been a change of letter but this mustn't or must not or couldn't change the meaning of the sentence." Do you remember giving that testimony yesterday? Again, page 39, lines 1 through 5.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I remember that. As I read my handwriting today, or say otherwise when I write things out, sometimes I just see it's different. It's just something that I do automatically but it doesn't really change the meaning of a sentence. I think that it happens to all of us; at least that's what I think.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: How about changing, adding a letter? Would that, sir, because when you took down the identification of the participants in a conversation you would usually use one letter to identify them. Such as K for Krstic; correct? Now, what if you were to add a different letter to the name, to that initial, that could alter and significantly change who the participants were in that conversation; correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, could it? As for the further sequence of transmitting information from the tape to paper, every time Krstic speaks, a K is put, or for somebody else, and then the first letter. It would be impossible not to notice that kind of mistake. I think that would be impossible. If someone made a mistake of that kind, you'd have to notice later on. I could not make that kind of mistake. I think that would be impossible.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I'm not suggesting you did, sir. However, if we could have IC 00041 be placed on e-court, please? Now, sir, my question -- while that's being done, I have a question. What I'm saying, sir, is that given that you use letters to identify a speaker, a change in a letter could indeed change not the meaning of the sentence but it could indeed change who the speaker actually was, like the letter B, for Badem, and if you add another letter to it, it could absolutely change the entirety of who the purported speaker was in a conversation. Don't you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, one moment before you answer the question. Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: For this witness, it's completely speculative. It's talking about -- the witness has already made clear and we have stated it with other operators that they can't talk about intercepts that were taken by other people. There is a completely speculative exercise that he's going through, and I object. The witness cannot intelligently comment on this which has nothing to do with him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Our attention is being drawn to the fact that the document you've referred to is under seal, but -- or a confidential document in any case. But however, Mr. Nicholls' objection is perfectly in order. You can of course, ask the witness as far as he is concerned, as far as any of his own transcripts, all right? If he -- whether he ever did that, and if he did, what would be the consequences, according to him, or his understanding of the issue. But please don't ask him about transcripts prepared by others for whom he's not answerable.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Very well, Your Honour. May I proceed?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, given your experience and your A certification as an amateur radio ham operator, can you tell us whether it would be a deviation from any of those standards or protocols that you have experienced and trained under if an intercept operator would alter, change, or modify a letter in the intercept book from a letter B to hypothetically a letter B and then adding a small E next to it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would like to make one point clear first. When a conversation is being transcribed from the tape to the notebook, if it is known who the participants are, then automatically, under the header, it is stated who the participants in the conversation were, and if we knew who they were, then it would be written down, the participants were so and so, with their full names, so I think there could be no confusion in that respect. However, later, when only one letter was used, then perhaps some changes could have been made. If we didn't know who the participants were, then they were given numbers and they were transcribed with numbers. But when we knew the names, then their names would be indicated at the beginning on top, Krstic, Popovic, and then later on, in the text, it would have just the initial.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: And you agree with me, don't you, sir that in fact placing in the upper section of that intercepted conversation when you identify the participants, that it was your -- fair enough. He doesn't have a translation, I think he said, Your Honour, I'm sure he said.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I didn't want to translate it. I thought they were. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Can you repeat then please.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, am I correct in that's why it's very important that the names of the purported participants in the conversation be listed plainly on the top section of the conversation that the intercept operators were listening to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is important if we know, and if we don't know, then we write down what we do know.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Have you ever, sir, seen an intercept which was altered or modified in approximately no less than 15 occasions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Can you, sir, agree with me that an intercept that has no less than 15 changes, modifications, or alternations is an intercept that is not reliable; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: How can you ask that question to the witness, without giving him indication of what the 15 alterations are?

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, because I restricted from showing him the 15 alternations --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Then don't put the question. Make a submission later on when the time comes.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: However, I think given his -- if I may, given his experience, and I don't want to go through his details, where he was exactly, the time that he was given, his role with the other operators, I think he can answer that, what he would do if his operators made those types of changes or alterations.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yeah, but it all depends on what the alterations are.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: But I think that this witness can tell us that, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No, I don't think he can, unless he knows what the alternations are. Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Just again, Your Honour, I think it's an effort to go around your ruling which was clear. It's still trying to get him to speculate. I don't agree with the characterisation in the first place, and I'd ask that he move on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I still think the witness would have provided us with an answer, but anyway -- but I don't think it's the case of putting the question to the witness, not in the way you have.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I'll restate the question, Your Honour, I'm almost complete, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, being in your capacity that you described for us, did you ever discipline or punish any intercept operators who would alter, change or modify, to any extent, the intercepted conversations that were recorded in the logbook similar to the one sitting to your right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never did I do that, nor did I have any need to do that. I never established that changes or alterations had been made.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, were there any guidelines or protocols in place that would enforce any type of sanction, punishment or discipline to an operator who would change, alter or modify an intercepted conversation in the logbook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can answer this question.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: It's just the issue is what is meant by change, alter or modify, and --

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: I think we can -- if -- I don't want to respond, but I think we can discuss semantics. However, if the witness doesn't understand what it means, the witness is invited to have this explained to him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm soon going to tell you whether he understands or not, Mr. Ostojic. If in a transcript I'm taking the transcript down and I have a letter starting with a small A and I change that small A into a capital A, would you consider it a modification of the transcript? Or ignore it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't consider that to affect the content. It is incorrectly noted but it doesn't change anything. Whether it's small or capital, the meaning remains the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So what you have in mind, when you are answering the questions put to you by Mr. Ostojic, is changes of material importance? Is that correct? Material changes, material alterations.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. But a -- changing a capital or a small letter doesn't change the meaning in any way. The meaning remains the same. It's just that the writing is not the same. And many of us can make errors of that kind.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. One other question before you conclude, Mr. Ostojic. Once a first transcript has been made of an intercept, before it goes to the person who will input it then into the computer, is the tape recording verified again, listened to again, in order to verify the transcript or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no. That wasn't done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you, yes, Mr. Ostojic, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, sir, I'm talking about material changes, but -- that are made in a logbook. Do you agree with me that it's a material change to change from a letter identifying a person with the letter B and then subsequently to add a different letter to further identify an individual? Would that be a change in your opinion, given your background and training from a B simply to a "Be"?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, we are now strolling down the speculative path. He had abandoned that. That's not the question he was asking before, I believe, but about sanctions or something of that nature.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not exactly speculative, but it all depends on the particular transcript. Because if you read -- when you read the particular transcripts you have no other options but to understand B and Be to mean the same, one and the same person, then obviously, there is no material change.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I don't want to.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm not saying it is so, but I'm just explaining to you that it is actually each and every particular transcript that one has to look at and you cannot ask that question in a vacuum, as if it would apply across the board to all the transcripts that we have here in these several notebooks that we have in the records.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: May he answer the question, Your Honour? Or no?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I don't think he should answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough. I'll ask another question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, are you familiar with the name of an officer by the name of Ljubo Bojanovic with a B?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, not now.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Now, sir, if an intercept operator recorded that person's name Ljubo Bojanovic as Vojanovic, would that change in one letter make a difference as to who may or may not be speaking in a conversation that an intercept operator was listening to, if the only reference to that individual was by his first name, Ljubo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If he was mentioned as Ljubo and if that was noted down, we would usually just write the name used. We never referred to Krstic by name, nor to Mr. Popovic. We would just put Popovic or Krstic. So that was my practice, so I have nothing concrete to add. If it's Ljubo Ljubo, I don't know which Ljubo.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I hate to interrupt. But, again, there is a big difference if there are two persons, one with one surname and another one with another.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: There is actually evidence that --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: There is only one person that can be identified within a certain context and it's only one. So ...

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough, Your Honour, I'll move on. And I appreciate it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is why I'm telling you it all depends on the particular transcript that you would be referring to.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And if the gentleman hasn't even ever heard of the person whose name and surname you mentioned, I suppose it's very difficult for him to answer the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Fair enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Sir, a question I think that you didn't answer, or I didn't understand the answer, and that is: Was there any protocol or any guidelines for disciplining intercept operators for making mistakes, changes or alterations in a logbook? I'm not asking if you actually did it. I'm asking you was there a set of guidelines for disciplining them if they committed such errors or mistakes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Sorry to object again, but if it's -- if we are talking about mistakes it's important not to lump those in with alterations or changes, and once again my friend is doing that. There wouldn't necessarily be any sanction, not that we've seen mistakes, but there wouldn't be any sanction for making an alteration obviously to make something more accurate, so I think he's got to break it down and be clearer in his questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think we can move to the next question, Mr. Ostojic.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Okay. I just want to know if there were. I'll ask it.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Were there any guidelines at all to discipline intercept operators for any reason whatsoever in July and August 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: They didn't exist throughout the period we were working on this job, not just in July and August, they never existed.

utterances.speaker: MR. OSTOJIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour, that's all I have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Mr. Ostojic. Who is next? Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I hope to make this short. Most of the questions I wanted to ask have already been asked. I'll try to make it as short as possible. I'd like to refer the witness immediately to the Exhibit 1138 Echo, on page 2.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: While they prepare this, good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Witness, looking at the exhibit that is in front of you, if you go down at the bottom of the page, and I would like you to look at the third paragraph, which is attributed to participant number 1. And I would ask you to read this paragraph out loud.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: "So this phantom, one of Oric's, some deputy, Zulfo Kasumovic, he pushed through via Konjevic last night and up there near Pasarda, somewhere, they are expecting him to pass with some 300 men." Is that what you were referring to?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness. Now I'd like to move on and to direct your attention to Exhibit 1138 Bravo on page 2. And if you look at the top of the page, the second paragraph attributed to speaker number 1, can you read this for yourself and confirm that this is the same paragraph that was entered into the computer from the notebook, the paragraph that you just read before?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, if I look at the notebook as well as the paragraph that was entered in the computer, it appears that when you read this, that there was absolutely no difficulties encountered in transcribing this intercept; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We can take note of that.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: So I don't see any mention, either in the notebook or in the computer-generated version of this paragraph, that there were either difficulties encountered or, for example, that this specific paragraph had to be listened to by many operators.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There is nothing to point to any difficulties being encountered in understanding. Everything was clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, I'd like to direct your attention now to Exhibit 1138 Alpha, on the first page. Now, sir, this exhibit is not in your language, but I will draw your attention to the bottom of the page, to the first paragraph which is attributed to speaker number 1. If we go to the bottom of the page, and we look at the first paragraph attributed to speaker number 1, now, I will read this for you in English, and you can tell me if that is the same paragraph that you just referred to earlier. "Well, that phantom, some deputy of Oric's, Zulfo Kasumovic, pushed through last night over Konjevic and they expect him somewhere up near," this word could not be understood, "to cross with about 300 men." Is that the same paragraph, sir?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it appears to be so, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Now, my question to you is very simple: You indicated that in your version, in the notebook and the computer-generated version, that there were no difficulties encountered in understanding this paragraph or in transcribing the paragraph. Now, the latest version that we have in front of us was generated by the translation people of this Tribunal, and when they listened to the tape they could -- there was a word that they could not understand. Could you explain why that would be so?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One, I don't see how this witness can be asked about queries the CLSS have put in. Two, what we are looking at is not CLSS listening to a tape. It's CLSS translating documents, so the question is completely off the point. Those are my objections.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Excuse me, Mr. President, just to clarify that, CLSS knows of the villages in the area, they are trying to be helpful and they are offering a known village as opposed to this the way it was spelled out in the intercept. That's CLSS doing that. They do that occasionally, and it's a practice that we've tried to dissuade them of but it's throughout some of these intercepts. That's what's going on here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Bourgon, before we decide.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Mr. President, it's quite -- yesterday we went over this intercept and this document, meaning 1138 Alpha, and it was explained to us that this was made from the tape by the people from this Tribunal. Whether it's CLSS or somebody else, this was somebody, something made from Tribunal staff or Tribunal resources. And my question to the witness is very easy. I'm just telling him that he indicated to us two paragraphs which he says they were absolutely clear, no problems in transcribing, and here we have a document done by somebody else, doesn't have to be the Tribunal, and they have problems understanding it. I'm just asking the witness what is the difference between the two and how come what he -- something that he figures was clear was listened by other people and was not clear.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: One, hypothetically if what my friend was saying was correct, there is no way the witness could answer because he wouldn't know what the quality of the tape was that the second translation was coming from. Second, if we look at 1138A, that is a translation of the printout, 00727582. 00727582 is on the bottom of 1138A, indicating it is a -- from the printout. There was one and only transcript made by CLSS from a tape that I talked about yesterday, and that is the tape we played which has nothing to do with this intercept.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Still, it doesn't change much in reality. How can you expect the witness to account for someone else who may have listened to the same tape and not under -- not have understood one word the same as or as much as he understood it? Where does it get you? Where does it lead us? How much would we have profited from it at the end of the day, Mr. Bourgon?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. For us it's simply an example that what may have been thought clear in 1995 may not be so clear when you listen to the original, but I will withdraw the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And I will move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But earlier on following a question from Mr. Zivanovic, I thought he was referring to previous transcript, previous testimony, while Judge Prost understood that it was a statement to the Office of the Prosecutor. So I was mistaken; she was right. How did that happen? It happens. So it's --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE PROST
utterances.text: Very unusual.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Bourgon.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I move on to my next question.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, looking at the exhibit that is now in front of you on the screen, I see that -- and you referred to that in your testimony, that the second participant in this conversation could not be heard at all. Can you explain or simply confirm that this could happen for many technical reasons that you can only hear one of the two participants.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's not technical reasons but simply it would happen often. If you review the tapes and notebooks, or these typed reports, you will frequently come across this because it depended on the link used by participant number 2. He didn't pass through that particular radio relay station. He just had a connection to it or in some other way. He simply couldn't be heard. Not because we didn't have the equipment to hear him; for some other reasons, he couldn't be heard. And I don't know what those reasons were. I can't explain now. But it is a fact that we didn't hear him, not just him but many others too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Also if I look always at the same exhibit, where the participant cannot be heard I see that there are three dots. Can you confirm that, of course, this does not allow us to determine the length or the duration of the response that was offered by participant 2 every time the first speaker said something?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, because we never checked on the watch to see how long people were talking for. We never made a record of how long a conversation lasted.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: And, of course, sir, you will agree with me that depending [B/C/S interpretation coming over English channel].

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you interpret for us, Mr. Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter apologises.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: These things happen. You see, can you explain, Mr. Bourgon, why that happened? I think, Mr. Bourgon, you need to repeat. I think you need to repeat because --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: I take my question again?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President. I'm sorry I missed this. I wasn't wearing the --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I could hear you, but then the translation into B/C/S disturbed me and I couldn't follow one or the other then. Yes, Mr. Nicholls, any objection?

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: No. Just, sorry, if we are going to continue on this exhibit, it might be better if it's in the witness's language, if he's going to keep asking him questions about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: It's not required at all, Mr. President, that he sees any exhibit whatsoever. Now that we have determined that once a speaker is not heard, we don't know for how long he spoke in response to each question or each intervention by somebody else, and my question was quite --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At best he could possibly give you an answer, if he remembers in relation to one or two transcripts, but certainly not all the transcripts that you may be interested in.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Absolutely, Mr. President. But the question is very clear.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Depending on how I fill in the blanks of participant 2, this will change very much the meaning and the importance of any given exhibit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And you're asking --

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Is that correct, sir?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You're asking him to replace our judgement when we receive an appropriate submission from you, along these lines. How can he answer that question?

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Mr. President. I move on to my next question, which is my last question too.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Sir, you referred to the fact that code-names were used and that with time you could manage to determine what these code-names meant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Which side are you referring to? In my unit or ...

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Let me clarify my question. In the conversations that were intercepted and transcribed, those people involved in those conversations sometimes used code-names, and I just want you to confirm that with times in your testimony you said that you managed to determine what these code-names meant; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would put it this way: In our work, we were primarily interested in what we were hearing, to put that down on paper, and send it where we had to send it to. We didn't go into code-names, secret names, but I do know from serving in the former JNA and as an active participant until the outbreak of the war in 1992, I was a non-commissioned officer in communications, I knew the rules of the army, and the army used code-names, so that in the process of work, we found out about certain code-names of individual persons, but this was not something that we needed for our work, nor did we give that matter any serious thought. There was a sector attached to the command for analysis, and on the basis of all those intercepts they created a picture of the system of command, of the deployment of units, and everything else in the area that was being monitored.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. That was exactly what I was trying to get at. And my question is: Can you confirm that during the time that you performed those duties that you referred to during your testimony, you were not able to determine whether these code-names changed from the beginning until the end of the war?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is something that I never thought about. And I didn't really notice that they did change, actually. But I'm not claiming anything. I didn't give this any thought, and I cannot give a specific answer.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: My last question, sir. Based on your testimony and the instructions that you were given to perform your duties, I would just like to know that if you intercepted a conversation in which a person bearing the name White used the name White, White is what you would find in the transcript and the notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. We wrote down what we heard. In principle, that was our mode of operation.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you very much, sir. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: MR. BOURGON
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you so much.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, too.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, Witness.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like us to clarify a few matters. Yesterday, if you remember, you mentioned Paket communications. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you tell me what you mean by that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Paket communications is a mode of communication between two operators by way of a computer, a modem, a radio, and an antenna. There have to be two operators with two full sets. One operator would have one set, and the other operator would have the other set. To this day, ham radio operators use that. You can ask people here in The Hague too. I saw one of them here today. And I can tell you what it means too. That means that if you provide a computer with information, that is the so-called digital repeater communication. That's what we called it. And now, these two computers are communicating between themselves. Due to interference and everything else, if it goes on for a long time, it would be susceptible to interference from other signals, other stations, so the question is whether the information would be conveyed to the next computer as it was given originally. However, then the computer has its own software and then it divides your information into several packets, depending on the length of the text.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we've heard enough, and I'm sure you've heard enough. Mr. Stojanovic, your next question. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: We don't want to go into those technical aspects because, objectively speaking, we cannot follow you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: But I am ready to provide this.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: As for this Paket communication between two computers, or two participants, do you need to have radio relay communication between these two participants?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, you see, if these two participants are working from two valleys and there is a hill between them, then you need this digital repeater, this particular device that conveys or transmits the message. However, we had optical connections with the corps command. We did not need any intermediary. We had a direct link between two computers that carried out this work.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That is precisely the reason why I'm asking about this. In 1995, in the area of the enclave of Srebrenica, there was a unit that was called the 28th Division of the 2nd Corps of the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And they had Paket communication with the 2nd Corps of the army of Bosnia-Herzegovina. My question is as follows: Did you at any point in time, (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I beg your pardon. Can we just redact the last words?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You could have gone ahead and we would have redacted them without mentioning it. So go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: You are at your position and did you play the role of an intermediary in this Paket communication between Srebrenica and the command of the 2nd Corps of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I've already answered that question. I answered it yesterday and perhaps I answered it today too. Up there, at the facility, there was a signals squad that perhaps did that and acted as an intermediary, and there were two or three digital repeaters, so it was through these devices that they could operate. They exist to this day. Nobody has to operate them. They just need electricity and that's it. But we were not involved in these signals. We just listened. My operators and I, we never uttered a word through any kind of communications equipment throughout our stay there. We were not intermediaries. We just listened.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Let me conclude on this.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It was my understanding that there was this signals squad up there that had a different job. Did you personally know that this signals squad in any way functioned in order to transmit these signals?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I didn't know about that. Quite simply, I wasn't interested in that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm going to make a standing objection to questions about this other squad which he's said over and over and over again that he had nothing to do with and didn't know whether -- where they were working.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Point taken and objection sustained. Please refrain from asking him to answer questions on the other squad or other group. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. That's exactly the way I put the question, whether he personally knew anything about that. And that concludes the matter.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Another thing I wanted to ask you about this chain, these notebooks that you used from the end of 1994, if I understood you correctly. These notebooks, up until the end of the war, did they get out of your possession; that is to say, 1995 -- until the end of 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: At the moment when a notebook would be filled out, the commander of the company, as I said, at the end of the shift would take a filled out notebook and fully recorded tapes for further processing down there, and I had no further contact with the notebooks or the tapes until here and now, when I have this notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So at one point in time, when it is filled out, a notebook, then it is submitted to your superior command?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Precisely. Where they were stored I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: I would just like us to finish with this question. Today in response to a question put to you by the Chamber, in terms of the first letter used, whether it's a capital letter or small letter, whether that changes the material status of a sentence, if I understood you correctly, you said that it was a question of grammar and that it was not really a fundamental issue for you. Do you remember that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: It's page 51, line 13, for the record, and line 18 of today's transcript, Your Honour. Knowing our language, and we speak the same language, I would like to give you a situation that can be a real situation or a hypothetical situation, but I would just like to deal with it, and I would like to you help us. In one intercepted conversation that one of your operators is listening to, one participant says: "Call Pop in Drinjaca and take the documents from him."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Before that, there is no further conversation, and afterwards there is more -- there are more things that are being said but that are unrelated. How would you transcribe it? I'm asking about capital letters and small letters.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I would probably act in accordance with grammar, I myself. I don't know. Should I tell you exactly where I would use a capital letter and where I would use a small letter?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would that mean that you would spell pop and Drinjaca with a capital P and a capital D?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Drinjaca with a capital D, because that is a particular place.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: What about pop?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Pop is not a noun.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Interpreter's note: That there is a double entendre here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Mr. Zivanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ZIVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would just like to have one clarification here. Is the word p-o-p, pop, used as a priest in the meaning of priest or as a nickname?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. In fact, the interpreters did hint to us that there was a possible double meaning to that word. I don't know which -- what you had in mind, Mr. Stojanovic.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I'm actually going to object, Your Honour. I would like the witness to finish today. I think his intercepts are in evidence, his handwriting, and we can see how he wrote sentences from them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps he can answer this question. He's telling me that he himself would have written Drinjaca with a capital D. And which pop are you referring to, Mr. Stojanovic?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, precisely. That is the answer to the question that you put and Mr. Ostojic too. In the language that we use, both the witness and I, the word "popu" can mean a nickname, somebody whose last name is Popadic, Popovic and the like, and it can also mean "to the priest."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The fundamental question is whether it's going to be spelled with a capital letter or with a small letter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Isn't it obvious that he would spell it the way he understands it and if it has more than one meaning, there is a possibility that he would understand it one way and I would understand it another, and Judge Prost would understand it other, and so on and so forth. And if I understood it to be referring to Popovic, I would put a capital P; but if I'm referring to pop, what our kids drink, I would not put a capital P. So let's proceed, Mr. Stojanovic, to more substantial matters.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour. That was the point of this question. Precisely. We would put a small letter or a capital letter in accordance with the way we understand things, and we can understand them differently. No further questions, thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I notice Mr. Nicholls, and I also notice Madam Fauveau. You stood up first, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I sat down at "no further questions."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, could we go into private session for the first question, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Certainly. Let's go into private session for the first or however -- how many ever questions you have.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We are in open session, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2315? It is the notebook 01077916. And I would need page 40, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, yesterday you talked about a conversation transcribed on the 13th of July apparently, and you've stated on page 483 of yesterday's transcript that when you went through the notebook you were able to see the dates, even though the transcripts were not made every day. Now I would like to know how can you establish the date with such preciseness if the transcriptions were not made the same day and if the dates were not inscribed the same day? Or every day?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I mean if I did not write something down, is it really important to establish anything? As for this conversation on the preceding page or somewhere nearby, there is the previous date and I think after this conversation there is another date too. I think that it's clear why this date was placed.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Right. Now, could we please take page 42 of this same notebook, please? Sir, you've told us that the 14th of July, 1995, that date was written by yourself in the notebook but you do not recall why you wrote this date. Is it possible to say that the conversation in question took place on the 14th of July instead of the 13th of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It would never be inscribed at the end, the date, and I explained this to the gentleman who was the first to question me. Or was it the second gentleman? I'm not sure now. That this was stated on the following day. And then on the 15th, there are no conversations in this notebook. The conversations are probably in the other notebook that was active at the time. Quite simply, you see that there are two days on which we do not have any text.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: In fact, that's exactly the case, when we take this example.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1138, please. 1138 B. And in English, it would be 1138-1.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have a version that is transcribed regarding the conversation that took place on the 13th of July. This document which was a printout, is this document from your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, looking at the middle, the way I see it here, well, I cannot say anything because I haven't got the header. I cannot say yes; I cannot say no.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And if you look at the initials that appear on top of the conversation of the 13th of July, 1995, would these initials -- right on top. It's on top. Above.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could we just lower it a bit?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's it. Yeah, yeah. She's referring to these, I think. Yes, go ahead, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Those initials, do they refresh your memory in any way? Could this document come from your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: The second initial, ZB, could perhaps jog my memory but I cannot remember the first one. I cannot remember anyone with those initials now, just off the top of my head. If I were to go through the entire list, perhaps I could find someone. The second one would perhaps lead me to something. However, this man came in the beginning of 1995, up to the facility. And it is possible that he was there at the time because if that is the material involved because the plan was not up at the facility all the time. He worked in other centres, and perhaps this document therefore comes from another centre.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: I just think it might be helpful if the witness can see the whole page of the document, if he's being asked what it is and where it comes from, or at least have a chance to read it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If I understood the witness well, it's not this document that he wishes to see but the one which has the heading, and it would help him distinguish from which location or which base it was sent and then he would be able to tell us whether it was his or not. He wouldn't even need to tell us. We would know.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll get back to it, Mr. President. I would like to precise where the document comes from, if the witness can identify it, of course.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this document, as it is here, could you identify it? Can you tell us if the document stems from your unit or not?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He's answered. He told you he cannot. He neither excludes nor confirms.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit P1138C? And in English, it would be P1138D.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, do you recognise this document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. This one has the name of the facility where I was.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, if we look at the report, the beginning of the report, we can see the words zone 2, then we see some abbreviations, then azimuth, frequency, 02, the time, and who were the participants. Is it exact to say that this report contains much more data and is much more precise than the transcriptions of the conversations that you had in your notebooks?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that's only natural, because I said that we only used the notebook as an auxiliary tool. It did not have to contain all the details as is contained here, the network, the particular piece of equipment, and then also on the basis of the frequency itself, that is when these things were added. There was no need for us to encumber ourselves by writing all of that into the notebook.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... with me, then, sir, that this document would be an official document, whereas your notebook is a -- more of an informal document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I would always want what I did. I mean, for me an official document is my handwriting and the recording that I made. As for what another operator typed out into a machine, from my notebook, well, he could have, but obviously sometimes he would type it differently. So I stand by my handwriting, what I entered in the notebook, and what I recorded.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. So according to you, you deemed that what is in the notebook, what you've transcribed yourself, is more precise, more accurate, than what we can find in the reports?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is the most accurate, what I wrote in my own hand. That's what I heard, and that's what I would then write down.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it correct to say that you can only vouch for the preciseness and the exactness of what was written in the notebooks when it only comes to your notebook?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Absolutely.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Talking about this particular conversation -- could the witness be shown the bottom of the page, please. In this conversation, we see the name Zoki. I know that you were already asked on this point. You already answered. But I would like to make a clarification. During the entire conversation, you were never able to hear the voice of this particular person called Zoki; is that right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Absolutely correct. And that is why there is no text under his numbers.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So you really don't know if that voice belongs to a man, for instance, the voice of Zoki, if it's a man, or if the voice belongs to a woman, for instance?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course we don't know. "Zoki, goodbye" is what his collocutor said. I didn't go into that, whether the collocutor is a man or a woman.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And is it exact to say that Zoki can be a nickname for a person called Zoran, who would be a man, but it could also be, for instance, a nickname for a woman called Zorica?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Again, we are straying past what the witness can testify about. He wrote down what he heard. He's made that clear and I don't see the point of these questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he can answer this question. He put Zoki and how are we to understand it? I mean it's being put to him that it could mean a man and equally a woman. So let's see whether he agrees or not. After all, he never heard the voice of Zoki. Go ahead. Do you agree that Zoki can refer equally to a man and to a woman? Although they wouldn't have the same name?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Shall we have the break now, Madam Fauveau?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Certainly, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. We'll have a 30-minute break, starting from now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1395F, and in English it would be 1395E.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, this is another conversation transcribed by yourself and we have an added portion; somebody listened to the tape later on and added something else. You've said yesterday on page 66 of the transcript that Uran was the code-name of Popovic's chief. Is it exact to say that you do not know what Uran really means and that you only presume on the basis of the text that you see before you that it would be Popovic's chief or superior?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I didn't say yesterday that I know that Uran is Popovic -- or, rather, Uran is the code-name of somebody but I didn't say yesterday that it was the code-name of Popovic, and that's what I'm saying now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think we have something wrong here. Madam Fauveau is not suggesting to you that yesterday you said that Uran is the code-name of Popovic. She is suggesting that yesterday you said that Uran is the code-name of Popovic's chief, the sefe of Popovic. And she is also then asking you to confirm that you said so not really because this was communicated to you officially, that Uran stood for this person who was the chief of Popovic, but because you assumed so from the context of this and maybe other transcripts. This is the question that you need to address your attention to and answer.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. It's clear to me now. I think I said something to that effect but I think I also added something, that I wasn't quite sure, because this code-name for Krstic is not customary. He would introduce himself loud and clear. So this code-name, though it was used in this case, is not one I heard often. Maybe this was the only time I heard it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And to answer the question: Were you aware of this code-name before you heard it the first time during this intercept, this particular intercept.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that answers your question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This was the first time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That answers your question, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness be shown Exhibit P2315, 2315? We are talking about a notebook, and it's on page 76 that I would like you to open it, please. 77, please.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, the conversation that you have before you took place at 1300 hours, and this conversation took place on the 2nd of August, 1995; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we now take page 80? Sir, the date on this page is the 2nd of August. It is written after the conversation took place, but you told us that the date was never written down after the conversation took place. How can you be certain that this conversation that we saw just a couple of seconds ago was in fact the conversation from the 2nd of August?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Your Honour, to, I think, correct what my friend has said, I believe what he said was he never wrote the date afterwards, not that it was never written afterwards.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't have a clear recollection of it, so I would rather not express myself.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let's proceed with his answer, if he can give it. If he wishes to see the previous transcript, we'll go to it.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's on page 71, line 17, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you think you can answer the question that has been put to you, Witness, without the need to refer to the transcript or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When talking about the date, it wasn't customary to put it down, but some operators transcribing the conversations in this particular case, he noted it down, and we can see looking at the notebooks that a date was indicated every two or three days but it was not a customary thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is basically a repetition of what he said before.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Can we then say that there was no rule as to the inscription of the date in the notebook?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think that is already implied in his previous answers. I mean, one person would do it one way, another person would do it another way.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me, sir, that in this case, it is not possible to establish the exact date when you read the notebook; the notebook does not allow us to establish the exact date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that through a systematic analysis of the notebooks, one could find out the more or less exact dates. So if it's not there, this does not necessarily mean that we can't make any conclusions. Looking through these notebooks, we came to the conclusion that those are the dates that we are talking about.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could we go to page 58 of the same notebook, please. Sir, you do see a date appearing here. It's the 20th of July, 1995. And afterwards, there is a conversation transcribed at 6.48 and another one at 7.04. Could the witness be shown the next page, please. And here we have a conversation that was transcribed at 12.55 and it is probably on the same date, on the 20th of July, 1995. Do you agree with me that it could still be the 20th of July, 1995?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: As we see on the previous page, because the -- a day begins at 00 hours.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the next page, please. Could you please scroll down a little bit? Thank you. Sir, on this particular page, there is no date, and this transcribed conversation took place at 10.50, and there is no date. Could you give me the date of this conversation, please?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Only if you give me the notebook. Then maybe I can answer your question. But if it says here 10.50, after the previous one, then it probably belongs to another day, but just looking at it like this, I can't tell you anything. You would have to is show me the following days for me to be able to come to any conclusions.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: So can we just assume that this conversation could have taken place on the 21st of July? It is quite probable, isn't it, that this conversation took place on the 21st of July?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That is an assumption, but to claim that is something else.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown the following page, please. The same conversation continues on this page, and if we go to the bottom of the page, there is -- there is -- nothing new was added. There is no new transcription. Can we please take the following page?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I could clarify something else in this connection, if I may.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Regardless of the fact that the -- according to the time, these conversations are not in order. This does not mean to say that those conversations were not recorded on the same day, because it depends who was the first to write down or to transcribe the conversations. What is important is when the conversations took place, but that doesn't mean to say that in the notebooks, they followed the same order. You will come across a conversation that was transcribed earlier, that appears later on. So we can look through page after page to see which day these conversations belong to, but the time need not follow in order. It is very difficult to make any conclusions by just looking through one page after another. I really can't say anything with certainty until I'm able to assure myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... had the notebook before you, if you had the notebook, would you be able to consult it and tell us?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Then it would probably be easier. I really don't see the purpose. It is the facts that are important.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... to give me the notebook, if you could just lend me the notebook for a few seconds?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, we are going to get no where if we go through the notebook like this. Where do you think we could go? This is already -- already the way he has explained it especially, in the last minute or so, it seems to me that one could delay entering into the notebook an intercept and it would on the face of it appear to have been following the one before whether in actual fact it may have been intercepted earlier, so it's -- and it will be marked accordingly. So at that point in time you can get a picture which is -- can become pretty confusing. But anyway, I mean, did you give him the notebook? Let's make it available to him. Look at these pages. We are at page 62. And you've been shown 57, 58, 59, 60, 61 and 62. See if you can enlighten us on establishing the dates but we don't want you to speculate.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To assist the witness, after the date of the 20th of July, 1995, which is on page 01077934, the first following date is inscribed on page 0107796 -- 956 and the date that appears there is the 2nd of August. So between the 20th of July and the 2nd of August, there is no other inscribed date.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: My feeling is that you can really get to the dates if you have then the -- what was referred to maybe the official communication of the intercept once it's transmitted via the Paket system to the command corps, because there it would have a heading indicating the date, the time when it is transmitted and everything. So I understood the witness earlier on to say that if you really sat down and did a thorough examination of the notebook, obviously comparing it with the rest of the documents that would help you understand, then he could possibly fix the date of each entry there. Yes, Mr. McCloskey.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: Just -- I won't say anything in front of the witness but the -- we can take at some point one minute or two and I can address the Court how the Prosecution's theory on how this will best be established and then we'll have an idea what we are arguing about.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Not now, perhaps.

utterances.speaker: MR. MCCLOSKEY
utterances.text: No, I understand.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps before the next witness testifies. Yes. Yes, are you in a position to enlighten us, Witness?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. Your Honour, we could only proceed in the way that you referred to; that is the only way in which we could reach the facts. All the material, all the notebooks, the other notebooks, and I'm sure that we would put this puzzle together properly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. I think you can take the notebook back from him, Madam Usher. Yes, Madam Fauveau.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Mr. President. Could the witness be shown Exhibit 1395B, and in English it's 1395A.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, we have a report here that you have forwarded this report to somebody. So can you tell us who did you forward this report to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I didn't forward this to anybody.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Isn't this a report stemming from your own unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not necessarily. I didn't send it so I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Maybe I was making -- maybe I asked the question in a perhaps difficult way. These intercepted reports, whom did you send those reports once they were finished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: We sent this through Paket communications to the command. It's probably because of this telephone number that it was sent to check, in a way, who this phone number belonged to or, I don't know. Well, it was just recorded and it was sent that way. It is well known who we sent this to, like all other reports, but -- it says here private conversation, so ...

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Sir, when you say that you would forward your report to the command, what command are you talking about? Is it the command of your own unit, or was it the command of the 2nd Corps?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, no, no. Only the command of my unit. I had nothing to do with the corps command. It is only natural in the hierarchy one knows the way one goes, to one's own unit, and then there is someone who is going to send it further on.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: The date on this report, 2nd of August, 1995, was this date inscribed automatically by the computer? Does the computer have a special programme that would put the date, or was it one of your men who would put the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I answered that question a long time ago. It wasn't the computer. It was the operator. As for the next file, he didn't have to type it out again. He could just copy it and perhaps set the time right, something like that, the number of the document.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that it is always possible to make a mistake and that it's always possible to write the wrong date? A typo is always possible.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: There could not have been a wrong date.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And why was it not possible to write an inexact date or, in other words, how is it that it could happen that one could make a mistake?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Quite simply, in the morning the first report would be sent with a new date, about the state of affairs on the previous day at the facility, whether there were problems or whether there were no problems. That report was always number 1. And if you look at all these transcripts here, you never have a transcript that is number 1. So the next ones are always 2, 3, 4, et cetera. So the first report, once it's sent in the morning, with that date, then there can be no further mistake. That is why I'm saying that it is impossible to make that kind of mistake.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: That's it. This first report that would leave, would it be possible that that report leave your unit with a wrong date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, let's assume that that even was the case. That first report never contained that kind of information. It contained information about us at the facility, so that could not have been omitted and there couldn't have been an oversight of that kind, as far as the other reports were concerned, even if the first one would have gone out with a mistake, but I never noticed anything like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it exact to say that at a certain point in time you received the order to inscribe a date, to put a date, before each conversation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I do not recall ever having received such an order. It went without saying, in the report, that it would contain a date or the date. As for the notebook, if that's what you're asking me about, we never received orders about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Very well. But, Witness, I would like to know the following: In this report, the date figures on top in the heading of the document, but afterwards there are no dates again before the conversation. In other words, it is not retranscribed again.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, yes, those are the conversations that were sent on to the command on that day. And it is certain that they were from that date. They wouldn't -- we wouldn't have kept something for two or three or five days and then send it so much later. It's not logical.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: And we have already established that in the notebooks the dates were not put. Now I would like to ask you: Did you ever receive an order asking you that you put in a date before each conversation? If you recall. Tell us if you recall this order.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not an order. That's the way we worked from day 1. That was the rule.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D117, please. And before this exhibit appears on the screen, sir, you said this was the rule and that you were working with this as of the first day. But in fact on this particular report, there is no date just before the conversation. Witness, can you please look at paragraph 1? We can see: "I hereby order the following [In English] reconnaissance of RRV, radio link communications, the original conversation is submitted literally as it was conducted with the following heading, date, frequency," and so on and so on. [Interpretation] Can you see on top of this document, on top, in the right-hand corner, that it is sent to your unit?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order has a date and a number. However, this is an order that was written for these two squads, for the northern and the southern facility, that is. This is an order that was sent to all, so I'm not saying that it did not leave -- reach my facility as well, but it also has a date, it has a number, and the place from where it was sent. So I don't know what you are getting at, and I really don't know what you want me to say.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, that was not at all my question. My question was to ask you if, according to this order, you were supposed to put a date before each conversation, that each conversation had to necessarily contain a date as well.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, that is possible, but it was never stated as concerns the notebooks. There was not a single report that was sent without a date and without a number. As I've said several times now, the notebook was just working material. So not a single transcript was sent, typed out and sent that is, without a date and without the time. The order was complied with.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, could you please take a look at the word, "I order," "I hereby order," before that word we can see that it is written: "[In English] Commander of the 2nd Corps, strictly confidential, number 8/468/2 of 16th August 1995, and in connection with the submission of PEB reports by the RRPC and in all these shortcomings and deficiencies and for the purpose of ensuring the maximum quality of submissions of the information collected by RI."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. But the corps commander never sent orders to such a small unit. He sent that order to my command, the command of my unit.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, what I would like to know is your -- to give -- I would like to you tell us about two words, deficiencies and shortcomings. Could you please tell us what those two words refer to, shortcomings and deficiencies?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I don't know specifically, but I assume that the command of my unit, when informing the command of the corps, perhaps had some shortcomings and deficiencies and then they were ordered to rectify that, and then this was sent further on to us, something from that order that was necessary at a lower level too. Specifically, I cannot claim anything.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Madam Fauveau, how much more do you have?

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I will try to finish by the end of the day but maybe I'll need ten more minutes tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I certainly do not intend to deprive Mr. Josse from the five minutes.

utterances.speaker: MR. JOSSE
utterances.text: We don't require it now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you. So can I ask you to try and finish, Madam Fauveau? To make everybody's life much easier? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'll do my best, Mr. President.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you just admitted that some shortcomings and deficiencies were possible. Is it possible that mistakes could have been made regarding the date?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in the reports.

utterances.speaker: MR. NICHOLLS
utterances.text: Asked and answered several times.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Nicholls. It's true. Let's proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've stated yesterday that you were a unit of the 2nd Corps. Is it right to say that at a certain point in time you were subordinated directly to the main headquarters of the Bosnia-Herzegovina army, ABiH?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I never said that, nor were we subordinated. Who said that?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, you've stated yesterday on page 27 of the transcript: "[In English] After all, we were a unit of the 2nd Corps."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, we were a unit of the 2nd Corps, but not of the command of the army of Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But I wanted to know if at a certain point in time you were subordinated directly to the General Staff of the ABiH.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Stop. He's already told you no.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Is it true to say that the Main Staff was able to give you orders directly to you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was never done. But objectively and operatively, it could do that, but it didn't.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: To you or to your superiors?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] To my superiors, yes, but the question is whether we received such orders, and I understand that to mean the unit of which I was in command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown Exhibit 5D142, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Witness, please take a look at this exhibit. Isn't it an order stemming from the command of your unit, the superior unit, to which you were subordinated?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS PW-130 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. STOJANOVIC
utterances.text: Could you please take a look at paragraph 2B. I know that we are talking about jamming conversations. I will not ask you anything about it because you've already told us on this but what I would like to know is this paragraph 2B mentions: "[Previous translation continues] ...
